reference.title: Review, Compare, Stage, and Commit Actions

section.title: Open
section.p: Use: Opens the selected file, folder, or submodule so you can inspect it before you decide what to do with the change.

Details: For files, the resource opens in the main editing area or in the relevant editor. For folders or submodules, the Git Client opens the resource in the tool that matches the resource type. The action does not change Git state and does not stage or commit the selected resource.
Scope: Selected file, folder, or submodule.

ul.li: Contextual menu in the Unstaged files area.
Contextual menu in the Staged files area.

section.title: Open in Compare Editor
section.p: Use: Opens a comparison for the selected changed file so you can review the exact edits before staging or committing it.

Details: The comparison shows the working copy version next to the repository version that Git uses as the baseline for the file. This helps you check added, removed, and modified content before you include the file in the index. The index is Git's staging area for the next commit.
Best Practice: Use this action before staging changes so you can confirm that the file belongs in the next commit.

ul.li: Contextual menu of a resource in the Unstaged files area.
Double-click a changed resource in the Unstaged files area.

section.title: Git Diff
section.p: Use: Compares the selected resource with its repository version.

Details: A Git diff shows how the selected file or folder differs from the version stored in the repository. Use it to inspect local changes without opening the full staging workflow. The action does not stage, discard, or commit any change.
Scope: Selected resource.
Accessible From: Git submenu in the Project view contextual menu.

section.title: Stage
section.p: Use: Moves the selected unstaged resources to the Staged files area.

Details: Staging adds the selected changes to Git's index. The index defines the exact content that will be saved in the next commit. Files can still be edited after staging, but later edits appear again as unstaged changes until you stage them too.
Best Practice: Stage only the files that belong in the next commit.
Accessible From: Contextual menu of the Unstaged files area.

section.title: Stage Selected
section.p: Use: Moves the selected unstaged files to the Staged files area by using the staging controls between the file lists.
Details: This action adds only the selected files to Git's index. Use it when the working copy contains several unrelated changes and only some of them should be part of the next commit.
Scope: Selected unstaged files.
Accessible From: Stage controls in the Git Staging view file areas.

section.title: Stage All
section.p: Use: Moves all unstaged files in the current working copy to the Staged files area.

Details: This action adds every current unstaged change to Git's index. It can include modified, new, and deleted files. After it runs, the next commit will include all staged files unless you unstage some of them first.
Best Practice: Use this action only when all current changes belong in the same commit.
Accessible From: Stage controls in the Git Staging view file areas.

section.title: Unstage Selected
section.p: Use: Moves the selected staged files back to the Unstaged files area.

Details: Unstaging removes the selected files from Git's index, but it does not delete or revert their local changes. Use it when you staged a file by mistake or when you want to split the current work into smaller commits.
Scope: Selected staged files.
Accessible From: Stage controls in the Git Staging view file areas.

section.title: Unstage All
section.p: Use: Moves all staged files back to the Unstaged files area.
Details: The action clears Git's index for the current working copy, but keeps all file changes on disk. It is useful when you want to restart the staging decision without losing any local work.
Scope: All staged files in the current working copy.
Accessible From: Stage controls in the Git Staging view file areas.

section.title: Discard
section.p: Use: Discards the selected local unstaged changes.

Details: Discard replaces the selected working copy changes with the repository version. For new untracked files, it can remove the files from the working copy. This action changes files on disk and cannot be used to create a commit that records the discarded work. This action does not affect staged files.
Best Practice: Use this action only when you are sure that you no longer need the local changes.
Accessible From: Contextual menu of the Unstaged files area.

section.title: Commit
section.p: Use: Saves the staged changes to the local repository with the message entered in the Commit message area.

Details: A commit records a snapshot of the staged content in the current branch history. Only staged changes are included. Unstaged changes remain in the working copy after the commit. The commit is local until you push it to a remote repository.
Best Practice: Write a clear message and include only related changes in one commit.

ul.li: Commit button in the Git Staging view commit message area.
Resource-specific Commit action in the Project view contextual menu.

section.title: Generate Commit Message Using AI
section.p: Use: Uses AI Positron to generate a commit message for the staged changes.

Details: The action analyzes the staged changes and proposes a commit message that summarizes them. It helps when the staged files contain several edits or when you want a concise starting point for the message. The generated text is inserted in the commit message field and can be edited before you commit.
Best Practice: Review the generated message before committing.
Accessible From: Toolbar in the Git Staging view commit message area.

section.title: Choose a Previously Used Comment
section.p: Use: Lets you reuse a previous commit message.

Details: The action fills the commit message field with a message that was used before. It is useful when you need a similar message for repeated work, but the message should still describe the staged changes in the current commit.
Scope: Commit message field.
Accessible From: Toolbar in the Git Staging view commit message area.

section.title: Automatically Push Changes to Remote Branch
section.p: Use: Pushes the committed changes to the remote repository after the commit is performed.

Details: When this option is enabled, the Git Client runs a push after the next successful commit. The push publishes the new local commit to the branch's remote tracking branch. If the push cannot be completed, for example because the remote branch has newer commits, you must pull and resolve any conflicts before pushing again.
Best Practice: Use this option only when you are ready to publish the commit immediately.
Accessible From: Toolbar in the Git Staging view commit message area.

section.title: Amend Last Commit
section.p: Use: Combines staged changes with the most recent commit or edits the last commit message.

Details: Amend replaces the latest local commit with a new commit that contains the previous commit content plus the current staged changes, or an updated message. Because the commit identity changes, amending rewrites the most recent commit in the local branch history.
Best Practice: Do not amend public commits, which are commits that were already pushed to the remote repository.
Accessible From: Toolbar in the Git Staging view commit message area.
